web_fetch_with_url.text:
That URL now redirects to platform.claude.com. Here's the page in three sentences:

Tool use (also called function calling) lets Claude call functions that you define or that Anthropic provides. The main difference between tools is where they run: client tools (including user-defined tools and tools with Anthropic-defined schemas, such as `bash` and `text_editor`) run in your application, while server tools (such as `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `code_execution`, and `tool_search`) run on Anthropic's infrastructure. By default, Claude determines on each turn whether to call a tool or respond directly, and you can steer this with your system prompt or the `tool_choice` setting. On cost, you pay for input tokens (including the `tools` parameter) and output tokens, plus additional usage-based pricing (for example, web search charges per search performed).

The article is **"Building effective agents"** from Anthropic's Engineering team, written by Erik S. and Barry Zhang and published December 19, 2024 (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents). The page says "Much of the tooling landscape described in this post has changed since December 2024."

**The two types it names are workflows and agents.** The article doesn't actually use the phrase "two core patterns." It says Anthropic groups all these variations as **agentic systems**, but draws "an important architectural distinction between **workflows** and **agents**":

1. **Workflows:** "systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths."
2. **Agents:** "systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how they accomplish tasks."

On when to use each, workflows give predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks, while agents are better when flexibility and model-driven decision-making are needed at scale. The article also notes that for many applications, optimizing single LLM calls with retrieval and in-context examples is usually enough.

stats_code_exec.text:
For the integers 1 through 10:

- **Mean:** **5.500**
- **Standard deviation:**
  - **Population** (divide by n = 10): **2.872**
  - **Sample** (divide by n − 1 = 9): **3.028**

**How I got these:**
- The values add up to 55, so the mean is 55 / 10 = 5.5.
- The squared distances from the mean add up to 82.5.
- Population variance is 82.5 / 10 = 8.25, so the SD is √8.25 ≈ 2.872.
- Sample variance is 82.5 / 9 ≈ 9.167, so the SD is √9.167 ≈ 3.028.

The numbers 1 to 10 are the whole set here, not a sample from something bigger, so the **population SD (2.872)** is the right one to use. Use 3.028 only if these values are a sample from a larger group.

**What it is**
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems. Using MCP, AI applications like Claude or ChatGPT can connect to data sources (e.g. local files, databases), tools (e.g. search engines, calculators) and workflows (e.g. specialized prompts)—enabling them to access key information and perform tasks. The setup is simple: developers can either expose their data through MCP servers or build AI applications (MCP clients) that connect to these servers. research.notes_preview:
## MCP definition and purpose

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications (e.g., Claude, ChatGPT) to external systems: data sources (local files, databases), tools (search engines, calculators) and workflows (specialized prompts). Official docs compare it to a "USB-C port for AI applications."
Architecture: developers either expose data through MCP servers or build AI applications (MCP clients) that connect to those servers.
Problem solved: the "N×M integration problem" — each client and server implements the protocol once, so integrations go from N×M to N+M.
Sources:
- https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/getting-started/intro
- https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol
- https://www.databricks.com/blog/what-is-model-context-protocol

## MCP origin: Anthropic, November 2024

Anthropic introduced and open-sourced MCP on November 25, 2024. The launch included the spec and SDKs, local MCP server support in Claude Desktop, and an open-source repository of servers (Google Drive, Slack, GitHub, Git, Postgres, Puppeteer). It is MIT-licensed. SDKs exist for TypeScript, Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, Go, PHP, Ruby, Rust, Swift and others.
Sources:
- https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_Context_Protocol
- https://tech-insider.org/ie/model-context-protocol-mcp-update-2026/
